items.title: 14.12 Experiments and data collection to test a hypothesis about air quality

blocks.text: Designing experiments to test a hypothesis about air quality involves careful planning, data collection and analysis.

items: Hypothesis: a hypothesis is first developed, for example 'the concentration of airborne particulate matter (PM2.5) and nitrogen dioxide in urban areas is higher during peak traffic hours than during non-peak hours', which can be tested by collecting air-quality data at different times of day.
Designing the experiment: the details, including the variables and the method of data collection, are planned; busy road sites and residential areas are selected for monitoring.
Data collection: data on traffic volume during rush and non-rush hours are collected and compared, using reliable instruments and methods.

blocks.prompt: Design an experiment to test whether PM2.5 is higher near a brick kiln than in a village 2 km upwind.
blocks.explanation: Hypothesis: PM2.5 near the kiln exceeds that upwind. Choose two sites at the same height, one 200 m downwind of the kiln and one 2 km upwind; use the same calibrated nephelometer or PM sensor at each; sample at the same hours on the same days for two weeks, recording wind direction and whether the kiln is firing; then compare the averages and the day-to-day pattern.

items: Testing an air-quality hypothesis: state it (PM2.5 and NO2 higher at peak traffic); design (sites, variables, instruments); collect data (rush versus non-rush hours) and compare.
